prompt.context: Our client is the sole utility provider in Washington state. It is regulated by the government, which allows it to earn a maximum of 10% of assets as income. Our client's capacity is 1 million megawatt hours (Mwh) per year. The government recently mandated that our client generate 10% of its capacity from renewable sources. The company has two options: 1) buy green credits from a 3rd party, and 2) set up a wind farm.
prompt.question: What should our client do?

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to build a wind farm?
What is the useful life of a wind farm?
What are the maintenance costs for the wind farm?
What is the cost of green credits?
Have credit prices changed over time?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — price has increased from $5/Mwh two years ago to $20/Mwh today (a 400% increase)

clarifying_info.q: What is the current utility rate charged to consumers?

framework: Evaluate economics of each option: upfront costs, ongoing costs, and annualized cost per year
Assess profitability implications given the regulated 10%-of-assets income cap
Qualitative pros and cons: flexibility, capital commitment, internal capabilities, regulatory risk
Government/political perspective: rate hike impact on consumers, conflict with energy consumption goals
Recommendation: hybrid or single option with clear rationale

questions.prompt: For each option, how much would it cost the client per year to fulfil the government's 10% renewable mandate?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that 10% of 1M Mwh = 100,000 Mwh must come from renewable sources, then compute annualized cost for each option. Wind farm cost should use straight-line depreciation over 30 years.

math.setup: Renewable requirement = 10% x 1,000,000 Mwh = 100,000 Mwh. Option 1 (Green Credits): 100,000 Mwh x $20/Mwh. Option 2 (Wind Farm): 100,000 Mwh x $2,000/Mwh capital cost, depreciated over 30 years (straight-line).

questions.prompt: If the client buys green credits, utility rates rise from $0.10 to $0.11. What would the rate be if the client builds a wind farm instead?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that a $2M cost increase produces a 10% rate hike (from $0.10 to $0.11). The wind farm costs $6.7M, so they need to scale the rate hike proportionally.

math.setup: Green credits: $2M cost → rate increases by $0.01 (10%). Wind farm: $6.7M cost → rate increase = ($6.7M / $2M) x 10% x $0.10.

questions.prompt: What are the profitability implications of each option, given the regulated 10%-of-assets income cap?
questions.guidance: Under both options, costs are fully passed through to consumers via rate hikes, so margins are unaffected on that basis. The key insight for the wind farm is that CapEx investment grows the asset base, which increases the allowable income ceiling under the 10%-of-assets regulation — creating an opportunity to earn more absolute income.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the most important pros and cons of each option?

categories.name: Green Credits — Pros
ideas: Easy to exit if regulation changes
Flexibility to switch strategies as market evolves

categories.name: Green Credits — Cons
ideas: Exposure to market price uncertainty (400% increase in two years, from $5 to $20/Mwh)
May not be able to pass all future cost increases to consumers
Quick fix — not actually generating green power within the state
Future supply of credits is unknown

categories.name: Wind Farm — Pros
ideas: Improves company image by genuinely being green (positive PR with consumers and government)
Grows asset base, increasing allowable income under the 10%-of-assets cap
More sustainable long-term solution aligned with policy direction

categories.name: Wind Farm — Cons
ideas: Requires additional expertise and internal capabilities the company may not have
Higher rate hike for consumers ($0.133 vs $0.11), creating political pressure
Risk of investment becoming obsolete if government eliminates the renewable requirement

recommendation: Hybrid model (preferred): Buy green credits in the short term to meet the mandate immediately, while investigating and planning for wind farm development
This preserves flexibility — if credit prices continue rising, the company can switch to the wind farm
It also buys time to build internal capabilities needed to develop and operate a wind farm
Alternative: Build the wind farm if the client believes sustainability regulation will only increase in stringency; the asset base growth and PR benefits support long-term value
risks: Green credit prices may continue to rise (up 400% in 2 years), making the hybrid approach costly
Wind farm construction could face delays or cost overruns
Government may resist the higher rate hike associated with the wind farm
Regulation requiring renewables could be reversed, stranding wind farm investment
next_steps: Assess the client's internal capabilities for wind farm development
Model credit price scenarios to determine the break-even credit price at which wind farm becomes cheaper
Engage with government regulators to gauge political tolerance for rate hikes
Explore financing structures to reduce upfront capital burden of wind farm option
